newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Albania unrest shows West's failure to aid reform.
newsitem.headline: Albania unrest shows West's failure to aid reform.

text.p: Civil violence in Albania highlights the failure of the West to match its support for reform in Eastern Europe with similar help to the volatile Balkans, regional analysts said on Wednesday.

Hundreds of riot police swarmed through the centre of the Albanian capital Tirana on Wednesday to stop opposition parties from staging fresh anti-government protests over the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.
Albania's former isolation as a closed Stalinist bastion means it has little in common with the rest of Eastern Europe, the analysts said.

"Albania is not just another country, it's another planet," said Kancho Stoychev, managing director of Gallup International in Bulgaria. "They still have problems of urbanisation faced by the rest of Europe in the 17th century."
But analysts said the West should do more to integrate Europe's poorest state.

"The whole situation of the Balkans, including Albanian matters, has been given insufficient weight by Europe," said Polish opposition parliamentarian and foreign affairs specialist Piotr Nowina-Konopka.
"It would be right if Europe was much more present, inlcuding in Albanian matters, to avoid a repetition of what we have seen in the central Balkans."

After the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe in 1989, waves of Western advisers, volunteers and money flooded into countries such as then Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Poland, to help in the transition to democracy.

Fabian Schmidt, research analyst at Prague's Open Media Research Institute, said the West had done more for Albania than any other Balkan state -- military assistance to Bosnia and Croatia notwithstanding -- but more help was needed.
"You still have a very primitive political culture which uses Western-type laws but really doesn't interpret them in the way which they were written," he said.
"The answer should be very clear help in building up democratic institutions."

Schmidt also said the West had failed to push sufficiently for democratic reform after last year's parliamentray elections, which were widely criticised as unfair. "Europe didn't really know how to react," he said.
In Budapest, Hungarian Foreign Ministry spokesman Gabor Szentivanyi said Albania's former isolation meant it needed more time to develop.
"Democratic institutions are in place but if they are not as developed there is always a tendency for radical expressions of opinion to take place," he said.
Investment has been slow to flow to Albania, partly due to its inability to absorb it.
Stoychev said there was concern in Bulgaria about the potential impact of events in Albania on the neighbouring Kosovo region of Serbia and the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia.
Other analysts said that if Albania's economic problems worsened there could also be migration to Italy or Greece.

Laszlo Valkai, head of the department of international law at Budapest's Lorand Eotvos University, said that if governments were concerned about instability in the Balkans, they should coordinate a large-scale aid programme, akin to the post-World War Two U.S. Marshall Plan, for countries such as Albania.
"Investment is not done by governments, it's done by companies. (But) if I were the U.S. president I would still try to deliver Marshall aid," he said. "Anything less is just hopeless."
